title: Working With the Coursebook

pts: Treat the coursebook as one input among several, not an unquestionable authority on what and how to teach.
Publishers write for a generic global class; no coursebook was written for your specific learners' profile (Unit 2).
Authority over the lesson stays with the teacher's judgement, informed by the book, not dictated by it.

items: For each lesson next week, write the aim in your own words (not the book’s heading).
Ask: does the book’s material achieve this aim for my learners?
Mark each page: use as is, adapt, supplement, or skip.
For each ‘adapt’ or ‘supplement’, write one line on what you will do.
After the week, note which decisions worked.
Do the exercise with a colleague teaching the same textbook.
Involve learners: ask which activities they found most useful last week.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Lesson 1 (reading passage): use as is, add a prediction task.
Lesson 2 (grammar exercise, 20 items): adapt, use 8 items and add a pair speaking task.
Lesson 3 (listening from audio CD, no player available): adapt, teacher reads the script.
Lesson 4 (writing task on ‘a visit to a zoo’): supplement, offer a local alternative (a visit to a market or temple fair).

body: Purpose: to position the coursebook among resources. Content: a teacher figure in the centre. Around her, in a circle: the coursebook (largest), learners’ lives, authentic texts, the board, learners’ home languages, digital tools. Arrows point from each to the teacher, not from the book to the teacher alone. Style: warm, clean. Board version: a circle of words around a stick figure.

items: DIKSHA (free). Many state textbooks are linked to supplementary digital content via QR codes; check what is available for your book. [VERIFY for your state and grade.]

blocks.x: Pencil notes in your own copy of the textbook: U, A, S, or X beside each activity.

pts: Omit what's unnecessary for this class's needs, however complete the page looks.
Add what's missing — often speaking practice or authentic listening the book under-serves.
Adapt what doesn't fit — reword an artificial dialogue, swap an irrelevant example, regrade a task's difficulty.

items: Choose one page you will teach soon.
Omit: cross out anything that does not serve the aim or duplicates something else.
Add: note what is missing (often speaking practice or a personal connection).
Adapt: rewrite one instruction, example or task to fit your learners better.
Teach the adapted page and compare it with how the unadapted version usually goes.
Swap pages with a colleague and adapt each other’s.
Adapt a page for two levels in the same class (Unit 15).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Adapting a page on daily routines:

lines: Omit: the second of two identical matching exercises.
Add: a pair survey, What time do you get up? How do you come to school?
Adapt: change the example character from ‘Tom in London’ to ‘Kavya in Tumakuru’, and change takes the Underground to takes the bus.

body: Purpose: to show the three adaptation moves. Content: a stylized textbook page with three marks: a line through one exercise (‘Omit’), a sticky note attached at the side (‘Add’), and a pencil rewriting one sentence (‘Adapt’). Style: realistic but simple. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Docs (free). Keep an ‘adaptations’ document for each textbook, one entry per page, to reuse next year.

blocks.x: Sticky notes in the teacher’s copy of the book.

pts: Check whether coursebook dialogues resemble real spoken language or artificially clean 'textbook English.'
Spoken corpora show real conversation is full of hesitation, overlap and incomplete sentences that coursebooks often smooth away.
Where authenticity is missing, supplement with real audio or video rather than relying on the scripted dialogue alone.
points.who: Corpus-informed critique; McCarthy & Carter on spoken corpora

v: A coursebook dialogue; a transcript of real conversation (see model language)

items: Learners read a coursebook dialogue aloud in pairs.
Show a transcript of a real, informal conversation on a similar topic.
Learners list differences: hesitations, short answers, overlaps, fillers, unfinished sentences.
Discuss: why do coursebooks tidy these features away?
Learners rewrite the coursebook dialogue to sound more natural and perform it.
Record two colleagues having an unscripted conversation and transcribe a minute of it.
Compare with dialogues in films.
Support: highlight the features in the real transcript.
Stretch: learners explain the function of each feature (well to hesitate, you know to check).

lines: A: Good morning. Would you like to come to the cinema with me on Saturday?
B: Yes, I would like to come. What time does the film start?
A: Hey, you free Saturday?
B: Um, yeah, think so. Why?
A: There’s a film, the new one, at the mall. Wanna come?
B: Yeah, sure. What time?

blocks.x: Features of spoken English often missing from coursebooks (McCarthy and Carter 1995): ellipsis (you free?), fillers (um, well), discourse markers (so, anyway), vague language (sort of, and stuff).

body: Purpose: to contrast scripted and natural dialogue. Content: two speech-bubble conversations side by side. Left, tidy full sentences in neat bubbles. Right, shorter overlapping bubbles with fillers and incomplete sentences, some bubbles slightly overlapping. Labels: ‘Textbook’ and ‘Real life’. Style: clear, not mocking. Board version: two short dialogues.

items: ELLLO (free). Unscripted recordings with transcripts, useful as ‘real life’ comparisons.

blocks.x: Record, with permission, a two-minute conversation between two colleagues on a phone, and write out the transcript by hand.

pts: Bridge generic coursebook examples to learners' own lives, work and interests to increase engagement.
A grammar point practised with the learners' own real information is remembered better than the same point practised with invented characters.
Personalisation costs little planning time and consistently raises engagement.

items: Take a textbook exercise with invented characters (Sam likes football. Maria likes music.).
Before doing it, ask learners to write the same sentences about people in the class.
Learners complete the textbook exercise quickly as a model.
Then they do the personalized version in pairs, asking real questions.
Share a few real facts with the class.
Replace a textbook reading about a foreign city with learners’ descriptions of their own town, using the same questions.
Let learners write the example sentences for next year’s class.
Support: provide question frames.
Stretch: learners report surprising facts about classmates.

lines: Textbook: Sam gets up at seven. He has cereal for breakfast.
Personalized: Ananya gets up at half past five. She has idli for breakfast. She helps her mother before school.

blocks.x: A personalized grammar practice: Find someone in the class who has never been on a train / can cook rice / speaks three languages.

body: Figure 13.4 From textbook character to real learner

Purpose: to show personalization. Content: on the left, a generic cartoon character labelled ‘Sam’ with a speech bubble. On the right, a group of diverse Indian learners each with their own speech bubble about themselves. An arrow labelled ‘personalize’ between them. Style: warm, inclusive illustration. Board version: not applicable.

items: Mentimeter (free basic version). Collect class facts anonymously (How many languages do you speak?) and use the results as material.

blocks.x: A ‘class facts’ poster built from learners’ answers.

body: Personalization is the cheapest adaptation there is. It needs no photocopies, no preparation beyond a moment’s thought, and it almost always increases engagement. Try it on any exercise with invented people in it.

pts: Coursebook grammar explanations are often simplified for teachability, sometimes at the cost of real nuance.
Corpus evidence frequently shows native-speaker usage diverging from the tidy rule presented on the page.
Supplement with corpus-informed nuance where the gap matters for the learners' actual needs.

v: A textbook grammar box; a corpus tool

items: Choose a grammar rule from the textbook (for example, ‘will is used for the future’).
Look up real examples of the future in a corpus or a grammar reference.
Note uses the textbook rule does not mention.
Decide whether the difference matters for your learners at this level.
If it does, add one sentence of nuance when you teach the rule.
Ask learners to collect examples of a structure from films or newspapers and compare them with the textbook rule.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A textbook simplification and the real picture:

lines: Textbook: Use some in positive sentences and any in questions and negatives.
Real use: Would you like some tea? (some in offers); Any child can do this. (any meaning ‘it doesn’t matter which’).
Decision: at A2, add the offer use (Would you like some…?); leave the second use for later.

body: Purpose: to show the gap between simplified rules and use. Content: a neat rule box on the left, and on the right a scatter of real example sentences, most inside the box’s coverage but some outside it, highlighted. Caption: ‘Rules are maps, not territory.’ Style: clean diagram. Board version: not applicable.

items: SkELL (free). Search a structure to see real examples.
Practical English Usage (Swan 2016) is a print reference many teachers keep for these questions.

blocks.x: A good grammar reference in the staff room.

pts: Most coursebooks under-serve listening and speaking relative to grammar and reading.
Plan deliberate supplementation for these skills rather than assuming the book's coverage is proportional to what learners need.
This is a known critique in materials-development literature, not a flaw unique to any one series.

v: A textbook unit; the skills audit from Unit 11

items: Audit a unit for skills balance (Unit 11).
Identify the weakest area (often listening and speaking).
Add one short supplement per lesson: a teacher-read listening, a two-minute pair talk, a song, a dictation.
Keep supplements short and tied to the unit’s language.
File each supplement with the unit for next year.
Build a supplement bank with colleagues, one folder per textbook unit.
Ask learners which skill they want more of.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Quick supplements for speaking and listening:

lines: Teacher story (3 minutes): tell a short personal anecdote using the unit’s language.
Pair interview (5 minutes): three questions from the unit topic.
Dictogloss (10 minutes): read a short paragraph twice; learners reconstruct it in pairs.

body: Purpose: to show supplementation. Content: a textbook unit drawn as a quilt of squares, mostly reading and grammar colours, with a few gaps. New patches labelled ‘listening’ and ‘speaking’ are being stitched into the gaps. Style: warm textile imagery. Board version: not applicable.

items: BBC Learning English (free). Short listening and video materials graded by level; choose items that match unit topics.

blocks.x: The teacher’s own voice, reading or telling, is the most flexible listening supplement available.

pts: Don't assume the book's unit order is optimal for your specific class — reorder around the needs identified in Unit 2.
Some units may deserve more time; others can be compressed or set as self-study.
A scheme of work (Unit 14) is where this reordering gets formalised.

v: The textbook contents; learners’ needs analysis (Unit 2)

items: List the textbook units and the needs identified in Unit 2.
Mark units that meet urgent needs and units that meet later ones.
Check any institutional constraints (exam dates, prescribed order).
Where allowed, reorder so urgent needs come first.
Record the new order in your scheme of work (Unit 14).
If order is fixed, reorder within units instead (for example, do the speaking task before the reading).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Learners have a school trip in week 4; the textbook unit on travel is unit 9. → Teach unit 9 in week 3, then return to the book order.

body: Purpose: to show flexible sequencing. Content: a row of numbered unit cards 1–10. Card 9 is lifted from its place with a curved arrow moving it to position 3. A small calendar icon above shows ‘school trip, week 4’. Style: clean. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Sheets (free). A term calendar with textbook units dragged into place.

blocks.x: Unit numbers written on cards and arranged on a desk before being copied into the plan.

pts: Dogme-inspired 'unplugged' lessons, built from learner-generated language rather than any material, have a real place in a course.
These lessons work best interspersed with coursebook-driven ones, not as a wholesale replacement.
Going off-book is a deliberate methodological choice, not merely what happens when the book runs out.

items: Start with a conversation: ‘What happened this weekend?’
As learners talk, write interesting language they produce (and language they needed but lacked) on the board.
After ten minutes, work on the board language: reformulate, correct, extend.
Learners use the new language in a second conversation with a new partner.
End by asking learners what they learned.
Start from a picture, an object or a news headline.
Alternate: one unplugged lesson for every four coursebook lessons.
Support: give sentence starters for the first conversation.
Stretch: learners take turns leading the reformulation.

blocks.x: Board language from a weekend conversation:

lines: Learner: I went to my cousin marriage. → Reformulation: I went to my cousin’s wedding.
Needed: reception, relatives, it went on till midnight

blocks.x: Teaching Unplugged (Meddings and Thornbury 2009) calls this approach ‘Dogme’: lessons built from learners’ own language rather than prepared materials. It works best alongside a coursebook, not as a total replacement.

body: Purpose: to show language emerging from conversation. Content: a board with learner sentences at the top, reformulations beneath with arrows, and a list of new words in a corner. No textbook in sight; a circle of chairs drawn below the board. Style: chalk-like, lively. Board version: as described.

items: None needed. That is the point of the lesson.

body: Teach one unplugged lesson this month. Afterwards, list the language that came up. Compare it with the textbook unit you are teaching. How much overlapped, and how much was language your learners needed that the book did not offer?

dek: Unit 13 of 100: a coursebook is a resource to be audited and shaped, not a script to be followed page by page — three moves make that shift practical.

aims.x: This unit is about working with the coursebook rather than for it. It offers ways to audit, adapt, personalize and supplement a prescribed book, and to recognize when a lesson is better taught without one.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: treat the coursebook as one resource among several;
apply the ‘omit, add, adapt’ moves to any page;
audit coursebook texts for authenticity;
personalize coursebook activities with learners’ own lives;
check simplified coursebook grammar against real usage;
identify and supplement a book’s weaker areas;
reorder units to match learners’ needs;
plan occasional lessons built from learners’ own language.

why: Why this matters. Most teachers work from a coursebook most of the time. The skill isn't rejecting it — it's knowing exactly where and why to depart from it.

background.x: For most English teachers in the world, the coursebook is the single most important resource they have. In many Indian schools, it is also prescribed: the textbook is chosen by a state or national body, and examinations are based on it. Talk of ‘going beyond the book’ can therefore sound unrealistic. It need not be. Almost every good teacher adapts the book, whether or not they call it that.

The arguments about coursebooks are old. Dick Allwright (1981) asked what teaching materials are for and suggested that they can deskill teachers if they take over decisions teachers should make. Others have pointed out that coursebooks save teachers enormous time, provide a clear progression and give learners something to take home. Both positions are right. The question is not whether to use the book but how.

Brian Tomlinson (2011) and John McGrath (2013) describe the teacher’s work with materials as a continuous process of evaluation and adaptation. The simplest framework has three moves: omit what does not serve these learners, add what they need and the book lacks, and adapt what is almost right. These moves need not be large. Replacing an invented name with a learner’s name, turning a reading comprehension into a pair quiz, or cutting one of three near-identical exercises are all adaptation.

For prescribed textbooks, adaptation works within limits. The content that will be examined must be taught. But how it is taught, what surrounds it and how learners meet it again are almost always the teacher’s choice.

items: Adaptation log. Keep a record of adaptations and learner response for one term; review which kinds worked best.
Personalization effect. Compare participation in a personalized and a non-personalized version of similar exercises.
Natural dialogue task. Learners rewrite a coursebook dialogue to sound more natural; assess use of spoken features.
Supplement impact. After adding listening supplements for a term, compare listening scores with the previous term.
How much of your teaching time follows the coursebook exactly? How much is adapted?
What does your textbook do well? What does it consistently leave out?
Which of your learners’ lives appear in the textbook? Whose lives do not?
Which textbook rule have you taught that you know is simplified? Did you tell learners?
What would stop you from teaching one unplugged lesson? Is that a real constraint or a habit?

Harmer, J. 2015. The Practice of English Language Teaching. 5th edn. Harlow: Pearson.
McCarthy, M. and R. Carter. 1995. ‘Spoken grammar: what is it and how can we teach it?’ ELT Journal 49/3: 207–18.
McGrath, I. 2013. Teaching Materials and the Roles of EFL/ESL Teachers: Practice and Theory. London: Bloomsbury.
Meddings, L. and S. Thornbury. 2009. Teaching Unplugged: Dogme in English Language Teaching. Peaslake: Delta Publishing.
Swan, M. 2016. Practical English Usage. 4th edn. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
Tomlinson, B. (ed.). 2011. Materials Development in Language Teaching. 2nd edn. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
perm: Coursebook pages and dialogues shown in figures must be invented, not reproduced from published books. Any recorded conversation used as material requires the speakers’ consent. Screenshots of DIKSHA, Google Docs, ELLLO, Mentimeter, SkELL, BBC Learning English or Google Sheets require permission or replacement with original illustrations.

terms.def: The quality of being genuine in origin or use: a text may be authentic because it was written for real communication, and a task may be authentic because it reflects what learners do outside class.
A published textbook that provides a structured sequence of material for a language course; teachers can adapt, personalize and supplement it rather than follow it slavishly.
A word or phrase that organizes talk or writing and signals how ideas relate, such as so, anyway, well, however or on the other hand. Spoken markers are often missing from coursebook dialogues.

An approach to teaching that minimizes published materials and technology and builds lessons from the conversation and language that learners bring to class (Meddings and Thornbury 2009). It is also known as ‘teaching unplugged’.
The omission of words that can be understood from context, as in ‘You free?’ for ‘Are you free?’ It is common in conversation and a key feature of spoken grammar.
A sound or word used to hold a turn or gain planning time in speech, such as um, er or well. Fillers are normal in natural conversation but usually absent from coursebook dialogues.

Changing published or existing materials to suit a particular class, by omitting, adding, simplifying, reordering or personalizing content; for example, replacing a foreign setting in a textbook dialogue with a local one.
Three basic moves for working with a coursebook page: leave out what does not suit the class, supply what is missing and change what remains to fit learners’ level, interests and context.
Adapting activities so that learners use the target language to talk about their own lives, opinions and experiences, which makes practice more meaningful and memorable.

Grammatical features typical of conversation rather than writing, such as ellipsis, heads and tails, discourse markers and vague language (Carter and McCarthy 2006). Textbooks often underrepresent it.
Adding materials or activities to a coursebook to fill its gaps, for example extra listening and speaking tasks for a textbook that focuses mainly on reading and grammar.
An approach, also called Dogme, that reduces reliance on published materials and technology, building lessons from the learners’ own talk and emergent language (Meddings and Thornbury 2009).
